analysis.one_liner: Makes the research tax credit permanent and raises tax breaks for US-based manufacturing research.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from November 2013 until that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the federal tax credit for research and development spending permanent (it currently expires repeatedly and must be renewed), and would raise that credit from 20% to 25% for research work contracted out to US businesses. It would also raise the domestic manufacturing tax deduction from 9% to 15% for companies whose research and development happened in the United States. The bill died in committee without ever being debated or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that spend heavily on research and development — pharmaceutical, technology, aerospace, and other manufacturing firms — would pay less in taxes. The changes are permanent for the research credit, locking in a permanent revenue reduction for the Treasury.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the research tax credit permanent by removing its expiration date, so companies no longer have to wait on Congress to renew it each year [S2] [S3].
Raises the research credit rate from 20% to 25% for research expenses paid to outside contractors when the work substantially occurs in the United States [S2] [S3].
Raises the domestic production activities deduction from 9% to 15% for manufactured products whose research and development substantially occurred in the US, through 2022 [S2] [S3].
The stated aim is to reward companies that keep research and manufacturing jobs in the United States rather than offshore them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the larger and permanent tax breaks, meaning either higher deficits or offsetting cuts and tax increases elsewhere. Ordinary taxpayers ultimately share that burden; they receive no direct benefit from the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives no offset for the revenue it gives away, so the permanent research credit and the larger manufacturing deduction add to the deficit or must be paid for some other way [S2] [S3].
The largest research spenders get the largest breaks in dollar terms, so the benefit concentrates in big pharmaceutical, tech, and aerospace companies rather than small firms.

Even the bill's supporters would acknowledge that tax credits reward research a company would likely do anyway, so a permanent credit can subsidize spending that would have happened without public money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for rewarding companies that keep research and production in the US, and the bill is targeted at domestic activity rather than offshore work. But the design is one-sided: it delivers large, permanent tax reductions to the biggest R&D spenders with no revenue offset and no accountability for whether jobs are actually created or kept. For most ordinary households, the direct effect is minimal — the main measurable result would be a larger federal deficit or pressure for offsetting cuts. Weighed honestly, the concentrated gains outweigh any broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Donna Edwards introduced the bill on November 19, 2013, joined by nine cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything new; the status quo held. Taxpayers avoided the bill's permanent revenue loss, and R&D-intensive companies continued claiming the existing, temporarily extended research credit as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no one gained

for.name: Rep. Donna F. Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make and expand tax breaks for US-based research and manufacturing.

for.name: 9 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Norton, Cummings, Tsongas, Cicilline, Welch, and Holt.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to break down; all ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee took no action at all, so the partisan shape of any opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would hand these firms a permanent research tax credit raised to 25% for contracted US research, plus a 15% domestic production deduction. Their gain comes directly out of federal revenue, with no direct benefit flowing back to households.

industries.industry: Contract research and engineering services firms
industries.note: The 25% credit rate applies specifically to research paid to outside contractors doing the work in the US, making contracted research cheaper for their corporate clients.
